practice.title: The Long-Game Prayer
agreedSteps: In difficult interactions — listening to a repeated story, dealing with bureaucracy, talking with someone who resists Dharma — make the prayer: as I am now doing this, may I one day satisfy this person with pure Dharma, and thereby be of true benefit to them.

Remember that Dharma means 'to hold back' — its bare minimum aim is freedom from suffering in future lives, not happiness in this life. Let this long-term view inform your practice and your prayers for others.
steps: Notice your cannibalistic demons — the people who challenge or frustrate you most. Remind yourself: these are my personal demons, they live in my pocket, and one day they will be my main disciples.
If Lamrim practice has lapsed, make a concrete commitment to restart it — daily Heruka practice and one Lamrim meditation, every day.
practice.quote: As I am now satisfying them with my blood, may I one day satisfy them with pure Dharma and thereby be of true benefit to them.

commentary.title: Do We Feel We Make a Difference?
content: There's a difference between believing we make a difference and actually feeling it. Believing it intellectually is fine as a start — but the real question is: do we feel it? When we genuinely feel that we want to make a difference, that we can, and that we are, a whole range of modern ailments start to fall away: apathy, nihilism, depression, low self-esteem, low energy. When we feel we're really making a difference, we feel inspired, uplifted, strong — not because it's about us, but because it's about others. That's what cuts self-cherishing.

Three phrases are worth using as a kind of mantra: I want to make a difference. I can make a difference. I am making a difference. Not just in this world, but in all of samsara. The point isn't naive positivity — it's about using real examples of benefit we've seen to fuel the wish for more spiritual power. We see what's possible even with our limited abilities and enormous bag of delusions, and we think: how much more could we do as we become wiser, more compassionate, more powerful?

commentary.title: Emptiness Is What Makes Difference-Making Real
content: In an inherently existent world full of inherently existent people, how in the world do you make a difference? How do you help inherently existent suffering as an inherently existent self? It doesn't even function. But if we think from the point of view of emptiness — if everything is the nature of my mind — then by changing my mind, my world is actually changing. I'm making a difference. How I'm seeing the world is making a difference. Because things are merely imputed. There's no other way, actually, to make a sufficient difference than by changing our mind.

This is why increasing our understanding of emptiness is one of the most powerful things we can do. The more we understand it, the more we'll feel the weight and meaning of every thought, every action.

commentary.title: The Middle Way with Buddhas
content: In Buddhist practice, we are always moving towards dependent relationship. Dependent relationship is the middle way. Je Tsongkhapa explained that dependent relationship is the best way to realize emptiness — it always cuts between extremes. There are two extremes with respect to ourselves and Buddhas. Extreme one: Buddhas do it all, we do nothing — a kind of passivity, or its more diluted form of blaming others for our problems. Extreme two: I'm going to do everything — a solipsistic mindset, self-grasping ignorance masquerading as Buddhism.

Even Buddhas rely on their spiritual guide. Look at Avalokiteshvara — he has Amitabha on his crown, always showing the aspect of relying on a spiritual guide. It's a sense of dependent relationship. We'll lurch between these extremes until we realize emptiness perfectly, but until that day, it's just nice to be aware of where we're leaning.

commentary.title: Never Use Dharma to Increase Your Delusions
content: Whenever we read a sentence from the Dharma, we need to ask: how am I going to use this to overcome my delusions? All Dharma is designed to do that. We never, ever want to use Dharma to increase our delusions. You can use any line to increase them — for example, reading about the enormous non-virtue of anger toward a Bodhisattva and concluding we should just give up because it's too late for us. That's increasing delusion. The purpose of Dharma is to destroy our delusions.

So we need a filter — like a lens, a prism — to look through any Dharma teaching: how can I use this to decrease my delusions? In the case of anger toward Bodhisattvas: use it to deepen regret for non-virtue and wish to purify more. Or use it to be more mindful of how we think about anyone, because anyone can be a Bodhisattva. As teachers, we have the additional responsibility of being skillful — not presenting Dharma in ways that will increase students' delusions, even when those teachings are inspiring to us personally.

commentary.title: King Maitribala and Our Cannibalistic Demons
content: In one of his previous lifetimes as a Bodhisattva, Buddha Shakyamuni appeared as King Maitribala — wise, charitable, and well-loved by his subjects. Five cannibalistic demons heard of his generosity and appeared before him begging for charity. When the king gave them gold and silver, they refused: we are cannibals, so please give us your flesh and blood. The king assented, and as he gave them some of his blood, he prayed: as I am now satisfying them with my blood, may I one day satisfy them with pure Dharma and thereby be of true benefit to them. When this king was later reborn as Buddha Shakyamuni, these five demons were reborn as his first disciples — and after hearing Buddha's first discourse in Sarnath, they became Arhats.

So who are our cannibalistic demons? The people who challenge us, frustrate us, exhaust us. They're ours — not someone else's. They live in our pocket. We bring them around with us everywhere. And one day, when we appear as a Buddha, they're going to be our main disciples. We came a long way from demonhood — and so did they.
commentary.quote: As I am now satisfying them with my blood, may I one day satisfy them with pure Dharma and thereby be of true benefit to them.

commentary.title: Dharma Means 'To Hold Back'
content: One thing to remember when thinking about leading people to faith in the Three Jewels is this word Dharma. It means to hold back — to hold back from the suffering of the lower realms especially, then of samsaric suffering, and eventually of self-cherishing. These are the three scopes of the Lamrim. Protection is one translation, but to hold back is the most precise Sanskrit meaning.

It's so easy to think of Dharma as a psychological salve for the pains of modern life — like it just softens the blow of living a modern, miserable life. And it can help with that, definitely. But that's not the intention at all. The intention is, at the very least, to help people be free of suffering in future lives. Attaining happiness in this life isn't even at the bare minimum — it is below the bare minimum, underneath the least aim. So when we make the King Maitribala prayer, we're not just wishing someone a nicer Tuesday. We're wishing them liberation across lifetimes.

commentary.title: The Lamrim Is Non-Negotiable
content: There is no path to enlightenment we can follow without at some point realizing the Lamrim is essential. There will be a day where we conclude that — and until that day comes, our path is a little bit closed up. There are blockages impossible to penetrate without penetrating the meditations of the Lamrim.

Everyone who has had a very long, flourishing practice does the same thing: Heruka practice and Lamrim meditation, every day. When I meet people who are very conflicted and struggling in their practice, I've never asked them what they're doing and had them say, Heruka and Lamrim — every day. There's never an overlap there. So the question isn't really which practice to choose. There's always been an answer. Develop some admiring faith in the Lamrim. Let it become something you salivate over.
commentary.quote: The best day to love the Lamrim is [yesterday, or a while ago]. But the second best day is basically today. And then after that, tomorrow.
